def: The process of putting software into use on a live system.
ex: The deployment is scheduled for Friday night.
nat: Automated deployments help us release code faster and with fewer errors.

mis.bad: We made the deploy yesterday.
mis.good: We did the deployment yesterday.
mis.why: 'Deploy' is mainly a verb; use 'deployment' as the noun.

def: A period when a system or service stops working.
ex: The outage lasted almost two hours and affected all customers.
nat: We need a better plan to prevent another outage during peak hours.

mis.bad: The system fell for two hours.
mis.good: The system was down for two hours.
mis.why: Use 'was down' or 'had an outage', not 'fell'.

def: The act of returning software to an earlier, working version.
ex: We did a rollback because the new release broke the login page.
nat: A quick rollback saved us from a long outage.

mis.bad: We need to make a roll-back of the version.
mis.good: We need to roll back the version.
mis.why: 'Roll back' (two words) is the verb; 'rollback' is the noun.

def: The time when a system is not available for use.
ex: We planned two hours of downtime for the database upgrade.
nat: Every minute of downtime costs the company money.

mis.bad: We had a downtime yesterday.
mis.good: We had some downtime yesterday.

def: A small update that fixes a problem in software.
ex: Install the security patch before the end of the day.
nat: The vendor released a patch within hours of the report.

mis.bad: Please make the patch in all servers.
mis.good: Please apply the patch to all servers.
mis.why: Use 'apply/install a patch' and 'to' the servers.

def: A weakness that attackers can use to break into a system.
ex: The scan found a critical vulnerability in the login service.
nat: Hackers exploited a known vulnerability that nobody had fixed.

mis.bad: Hackers explore the vulnerability of the system.
mis.good: Hackers exploit the vulnerability.

def: A temporary way to avoid a problem without fixing its cause.
ex: There is no fix yet, but we found a workaround for the bug.
nat: As a workaround, users can export the report manually.

mis.bad: We found a work around for the bug.
mis.good: We found a workaround for the bug.
mis.why: As a noun, 'workaround' is one word; 'work around' (two words) is the verb.

def: The main reason why a problem happens.
ex: The root cause of the crash was a memory leak.
nat: We ran a review to find the root cause before making changes.

mis.bad: The root of the cause was the network.
mis.good: The root cause was the network.
mis.why: Say 'root cause', not 'root of the cause'.

def: An event that causes a problem or disrupts normal work.
ex: The security team is handling a serious incident.
nat: Please write an incident report after the outage ends.

mis.bad: The incident happened by a bug.
mis.good: The incident was caused by a bug.
mis.why: Use 'caused by' to give the reason; 'by' alone after 'happened' is wrong.

def: An extra copy of data that you keep in case the original is lost.
ex: Always keep a backup of your important files.
nat: The backup runs automatically every night at 2 a.m.

mis.bad: I will do a backup of the files.
mis.good: I will back up the files.
mis.why: As a verb, write 'back up' (two words); 'backup' is the noun.

def: To bring a system or data back to its earlier state.
ex: We restored the database from last night's backup.
nat: After the crash, it took us six hours to get everything restored.

mis.bad: I need to restaure the file.
mis.good: I need to restore the file.

def: A security system that blocks unwanted network traffic.
ex: The firewall blocks all connections from unknown addresses.
nat: Ask the network team to open a port in the firewall for our new app.

mis.bad: The firewall blocks all the ports of the server.
mis.good: The firewall blocks all ports on the server.
mis.why: Say 'ports on a server'; don't use 'of' for this relationship.

def: A group of computers that work together as one system.
ex: We run the application on a cluster of five servers.
nat: If one node in the cluster fails, the others take over its work.

mis.bad: We installed a cluster in five servers.
mis.good: We set up a cluster of five servers.
mis.why: Use 'cluster of' to say what it contains.

def: An automatic switch to a backup system when the main one fails.
ex: The failover worked and users never noticed the crash.
nat: We test the failover plan every quarter to make sure it works.

mis.bad: We did the fail over test.
mis.good: We ran a failover test.
mis.why: As a noun or modifier it is one word: 'failover'; 'fail over' is the verb.

def: The amount of data a network connection can carry at a time.
ex: The video call was poor because we had low bandwidth.
nat: I don't have the bandwidth to take on another project this week.

mis.bad: I have no bandwidth of time.
mis.good: I don't have the bandwidth.
mis.why: Informally, 'bandwidth' alone means available time or energy.

def: The delay before data starts to transfer after a request.
ex: High latency made the online game almost impossible to play.
nat: We moved the server closer to users to reduce latency.

mis.bad: The latency is very high of the connection.
mis.good: The connection has very high latency.
mis.why: Say 'has high latency'; don't add 'of the connection'.

def: An event where someone gets into private data without permission.
ex: The company announced a data breach affecting a million users.
nat: A single weak password can lead to a serious breach.

mis.bad: They did a breach in our system.
mis.good: They breached our system.
mis.why: Use 'breach' as a verb or 'suffer a breach', not 'do a breach'.

def: To change data into a code so that only allowed people can read it.
ex: All customer data is encrypted before it is stored.
nat: We encrypt backups to protect them if they are ever stolen.

mis.bad: The data is criptografed.
mis.good: The data is encrypted.

def: Able to handle more users or work without problems.
ex: We need a scalable solution that works for ten or ten thousand users.
nat: The new architecture is cheap and highly scalable.

mis.bad: The system is escalable.
mis.good: The system is scalable.
mis.why: 'Escalable' is Portuguese; in English it is 'scalable'.

def: Extra equipment that keeps a system running if something fails.
ex: The data center has full power redundancy.
nat: Redundancy is expensive, but it protects us from single points of failure.

mis.bad: We have redundancy of servers.
mis.good: We have server redundancy.

def: To prove who you are before getting access to a system.
ex: Users must authenticate with a password and a code.
nat: The app failed to authenticate me, so I couldn't log in.

mis.bad: You need to autenticate first.
mis.good: You need to authenticate first.

def: A point in a process that slows everything down.
ex: The database is the main bottleneck in our system.
nat: Approvals have become a bottleneck for the whole team.

mis.bad: The process has a bottle neck.
mis.good: The process has a bottleneck.

def: To watch something regularly to check its condition.
ex: We monitor the servers 24 hours a day.
nat: The team monitors error rates after every release.

mis.bad: We acompany the servers all day.
mis.good: We monitor the servers all day.

def: To search for the cause of a problem in order to fix it.
ex: I spent an hour troubleshooting the printer.
nat: Start by troubleshooting the network before you blame the application.

mis.bad: I will troubleshoot the problem of the VPN.
mis.good: I will troubleshoot the VPN.

def: To replace something with a newer or better version.
ex: We upgraded the servers to handle more traffic.
nat: The old laptops should be upgraded before the new software arrives.

mis.bad: We upgraded the system for the latest version.
mis.good: We upgraded the system to the latest version.

def: To move data or systems from one place or platform to another.
ex: We migrated all our services to the cloud last year.
nat: The data was migrated overnight without any loss.

mis.bad: We migrated for the cloud.
mis.good: We migrated to the cloud.

def: The username and password used to log in to a system.
ex: Never share your login credentials with anyone.
nat: The attackers stole credentials from several employees.

mis.bad: My credential is wrong.
mis.good: My credentials are wrong.
mis.why: In this meaning, 'credentials' is normally plural.

def: Software made to damage a computer or steal information.
ex: The malware spread through an infected email attachment.
nat: Our antivirus detected malware on two laptops this morning.

mis.bad: The computer has a malware.
mis.good: The computer has malware.

def: A scam that uses fake emails to steal personal information.
ex: Employees receive training on how to spot phishing emails.
nat: The phishing message looked like it came from our bank.

mis.bad: I fell in a phishing.
mis.good: I fell for a phishing scam.
mis.why: Use 'fall for' a scam, not 'fall in'.

def: Following laws, rules, or standards that apply to a business.
ex: Compliance with data protection laws is mandatory for us.
nat: The audit checks compliance with security policies every year.

mis.bad: We must be in compliance of the law.
mis.good: We must be in compliance with the law.

def: A level or point at which something changes or starts.
ex: An alert is sent when CPU use passes the 90% threshold.
nat: Once the error rate crosses that threshold, the system starts sending alerts.

mis.bad: The threshold of errors is five.
mis.good: The error threshold is five.
mis.why: Use a noun modifier instead of 'of errors'.

def: The amount of work or data a system processes in a given time.
ex: The new storage doubled our write throughput.
nat: Network throughput drops at peak times because of heavy traffic.

mis.bad: The system has a low throughputs.
mis.good: The system has low throughput.
mis.why: 'Throughput' is uncountable; it has no plural and no 'a'.

def: A collection of data used for analysis or to train a model.
ex: We trained the model on a dataset of two million images.
nat: The dataset contains customer records from the last five years.

mis.bad: A data set of the clients.
mis.good: A dataset of clients.
mis.why: 'Dataset' is usually written as one word.

def: An unfair tendency that makes results favor one side or group.
ex: The model showed bias against certain groups of applicants.
nat: Bias in training data can lead to unfair decisions.

mis.bad: The AI has a bias to women.
mis.good: The AI has a bias against women.

def: A confident answer from an AI that is false or invented.
ex: The chatbot produced a hallucination and invented a fake source.
nat: Always check facts, because hallucinations are common in language models.

mis.bad: The AI hallucinated a information.
mis.good: The AI hallucinated some information.

def: The text you give an AI so that it can respond.
ex: A clear prompt gives you a much better answer from the model.
nat: I rewrote my prompt and added an example to get better results.

mis.bad: I made a prompt for the AI.
mis.good: I wrote a prompt for the AI.

def: To make a process work by itself using technology.
ex: We automated the monthly reports to save time.
nat: If you repeat a task every day, try to automate it.

mis.bad: We automatize the process.
mis.good: We automate the process.

def: To connect different systems so that they work together.
ex: We integrated the payment tool with our website.
nat: The CRM integrates easily with most email platforms.

mis.bad: We integrated the tool to our system.
mis.good: We integrated the tool with our system.
mis.why: Use 'integrate with' for connecting two systems.

def: To set up software or equipment so it works as needed.
ex: I configured the server to restart automatically.
nat: The VPN is not configured correctly on my laptop.

mis.bad: I configured wrong the router.
mis.good: I configured the router incorrectly.
mis.why: The adverb goes after the object: 'incorrectly'.

def: Still available but not recommended and likely to be removed.
ex: This function is deprecated and will be removed next year.
nat: Using a deprecated library can create security risks.

mis.bad: This method is depreciated.
mis.good: This method is deprecated.
mis.why: 'Deprecated' = not recommended any more; 'depreciated' means lost value (like a car).

def: Old and still in use, often hard to change or replace.
ex: Our legacy system is over twenty years old.
nat: Many banks still depend on legacy software.

mis.bad: The legacy of the code is bad.
mis.good: The legacy code is bad.
mis.why: As an adjective, 'legacy' goes before the noun.

def: Able to recover quickly after a problem.
ex: We built a resilient system that survives server failures.
nat: Resilient teams stay calm and adapt when plans change.

mis.bad: The system is resilient of failures.
mis.good: The system is resilient to failures.

def: To reduce how serious or harmful something is.
ex: We added extra servers to mitigate the risk of overload.
nat: The team acted fast to mitigate the damage from the breach.

mis.bad: We need to mitigate the risk to zero.
mis.good: We need to mitigate the risk.

def: To pass a problem to someone with more authority.
ex: If you cannot solve it in an hour, escalate the ticket to level 2.
nat: I escalated the issue to my manager because the client was angry.

mis.bad: I scaled the problem to my boss.
mis.good: I escalated the problem to my boss.

def: An official check of systems, records, or processes.
ex: The security audit found several weak passwords.
nat: We pass an external audit every year to keep our certification.

mis.bad: We made an audit in the system.
mis.good: We did an audit of the system.

def: The date or time by which something must be finished.
ex: The deadline for the report is Friday at noon.
nat: We missed the deadline because the client changed the requirements.

mis.bad: We lost the deadline.
mis.good: We missed the deadline.

def: A person or group affected by or interested in a project.
ex: We meet the key stakeholders every Monday to share updates.
nat: All stakeholders must approve the plan before we start.

mis.bad: The shareholders of the project must approve it.
mis.good: The stakeholders of the project must approve it.
mis.why: Shareholders own shares in a company; stakeholders are anyone affected by or interested in a project.

def: To discuss something to reach an agreement.
ex: She negotiated a better price with the supplier.
nat: We are negotiating the contract terms this week.

mis.bad: We negotiated about the price.
mis.good: We negotiated the price.
mis.why: 'Negotiate' takes the object directly, with no 'about'.

def: The amount of money planned for a purpose.
ex: We have a limited budget for new equipment.
nat: The project went over budget by twenty percent.

mis.bad: We are inside the budget.
mis.good: We are within budget.

def: A statement about what is likely to happen in the future.
ex: The sales forecast for next quarter looks strong.
nat: According to the forecast, demand will double by December.

mis.bad: The forecast of sales is good.
mis.good: The sales forecast is good.
mis.why: A noun modifier sounds more natural.

def: Not done or paid by the expected time.
ex: The invoice is two weeks overdue.
nat: I have three overdue tasks on my list.

mis.bad: The payment is late of two days.
mis.good: The payment is two days overdue.

def: To complete and provide what was promised.
ex: The team delivered the project on time.
nat: We always deliver high-quality results for our clients.

mis.bad: We delivered the project in the deadline.
mis.good: We delivered the project by the deadline.

def: To mention a subject or concern so people can discuss it.
ex: I raised my concerns about the timeline in the meeting.
nat: Several people raised questions about the budget.

mis.bad: I rised a question in the meeting.
mis.good: I raised a question in the meeting.

def: A way of dealing with a task or problem.
ex: We need a new approach to customer support.
nat: A step-by-step approach makes the project easier to manage.

mis.bad: The approach for the problem is simple.
mis.good: The approach to the problem is simple.

def: A limit or rule that restricts what you can do.
ex: Time is our biggest constraint on this project.
nat: Budget constraints forced us to reduce the scope.

mis.bad: We have a constraint of time.
mis.good: We have a time constraint.

def: Something that is more important and must be done first.
ex: Customer safety is our top priority.
nat: Let's set clear priorities before the sprint starts.

mis.bad: This is a priority of the company.
mis.good: This is a priority for the company.

def: To decide what is most important and do it first.
ex: You need to prioritize tasks when everything is urgent.
nat: We prioritized the bug fixes over new features.

mis.bad: I prioritized to finish the report.
mis.good: I prioritized finishing the report.
mis.why: 'Prioritize' is followed by a noun or -ing form, not 'to'.

def: To give a task or responsibility to someone else.
ex: A good manager knows when to delegate.
nat: I delegated the data entry to a new intern.

mis.bad: I delegated for my assistant.
mis.good: I delegated the task to my assistant.

def: The amount of work someone has to do.
ex: My workload has doubled since two colleagues left.
nat: A heavy workload can lead to burnout.

mis.bad: I have a lot of workloads.
mis.good: I have a heavy workload.
mis.why: 'Workload' is usually singular; use 'heavy' (not 'a lot of') with it.

def: An important point or achievement in a project.
ex: We reached a key milestone when the first version went live.
nat: Each milestone has its own date and owner.

mis.bad: We reached an important mile stone.
mis.good: We reached an important milestone.

def: Something that is needed or demanded.
ex: A university degree is not a requirement for this job.
nat: We are still gathering the requirements from the client.

mis.bad: The requirement is to have experience of three years.
mis.good: The requirement is three years of experience.
mis.why: Put the number before 'years of experience'.

def: A formal plan or suggestion for others to consider.
ex: We sent the client a detailed proposal on Monday.
nat: The board rejected the proposal because it was too expensive.

mis.bad: I will do a proposal for the client.
mis.good: I will write a proposal for the client.

def: The final result of a process or action.
ex: We are happy with the outcome of the negotiation.
nat: The outcome depends on how fast we react.

mis.bad: The final outcome result was positive.
mis.good: The outcome was positive.
mis.why: 'Outcome' already means result; don't repeat both.

def: To succeed in reaching a goal after effort.
ex: We achieved all our sales targets this quarter.
nat: You can achieve more if you plan your week carefully.

mis.bad: We achieved to finish.
mis.good: We managed to finish.
mis.why: 'Achieve' takes a noun; use 'manage to' before a verb.

def: To move an event to a later time.
ex: We postponed the launch until next month.
nat: The meeting was postponed because the client was sick.

mis.bad: We postponed the meeting to anticipate.
mis.good: We brought the meeting forward.

def: To promise to do something or give your time to it.
ex: I can't commit to a date until I talk to my team.
nat: The company committed to reducing costs by ten percent.

mis.bad: I am committed with this project.
mis.good: I am committed to this project.

def: Required to explain your actions and take responsibility.
ex: Managers are accountable for their team's results.
nat: We must hold everyone accountable for meeting the deadline.

mis.bad: He is accountable of the budget.
mis.good: He is accountable for the budget.

def: To work together with others to achieve a goal.
ex: Our designers and developers collaborate closely.
nat: We collaborated with a university on this research.

mis.bad: We collaborate to the partner team.
mis.good: We collaborate with the partner team.

def: A standard used to compare performance with others.
ex: We use industry benchmarks to measure our response time.
nat: Their results set a new benchmark for the whole sector.

mis.bad: We compared us with the industry benchmark.
mis.good: We compared ourselves with the industry benchmark.
mis.why: Use the reflexive 'ourselves' when subject and object are the same.

def: The total money a company earns from its business.
ex: Annual revenue grew by fifteen percent.
nat: Most of our revenue comes from subscriptions.

mis.bad: The revenues of the company is high.
mis.good: The company's revenue is high.

def: A document asking a customer to pay for goods or services.
ex: Please send the invoice by the end of the month.
nat: We still haven't received payment for the last invoice.

mis.bad: I will make the invoice to the client.
mis.good: I will send the invoice to the client.

def: A legal agreement between two or more parties.
ex: Both companies signed the contract on Tuesday.
nat: The contract ends in December, so we should discuss a renewal.

mis.bad: We closed the contract yesterday.
mis.good: We signed the contract yesterday.

def: To make a process simpler and faster.
ex: We streamlined the approval process to save time.
nat: The new tool streamlines reporting for the whole department.

mis.bad: We need to streamline up the process.
mis.good: We need to streamline the process.

def: To pay another company to do work for your business.
ex: The company outsourced its customer support to a call center.
nat: Many firms outsource IT services to reduce costs.

mis.bad: We tercerize the support.
mis.good: We outsource the support.

def: To make something easier to understand.
ex: Could you clarify what you mean by 'urgent'?
nat: I'll send an email to clarify the next steps.

mis.bad: Can you clarify me this?
mis.good: Can you clarify this for me?
mis.why: 'Clarify' doesn't take a person as direct object.

def: To help a new employee or customer get started.
ex: We onboarded five new engineers last month.
nat: It takes two weeks to onboard a new customer.

mis.bad: We did the onboard of the new employee.
mis.good: We onboarded the new employee.
mis.why: 'Onboard' is the verb; the noun is 'onboarding' (We did the onboarding).

def: The time needed to finish a task and return it.
ex: The turnaround for design requests is two days.
nat: We offer a fast turnaround on all support tickets.

mis.bad: The turn around for requests is two days.
mis.good: The turnaround for requests is two days.
mis.why: As a noun, 'turnaround' is one word.

def: An amount that is less than what you need or expected.
ex: There is a shortfall of two hundred thousand dollars in the budget.
nat: The shortfall in sales forced us to cut costs.

mis.bad: There is a short fall in sales.
mis.good: There is a shortfall in sales.

def: To use something you have in order to get a benefit.
ex: We can leverage our existing data to improve the product.
nat: The team leveraged cloud tools to launch in just a month.

mis.bad: We can leverage of our existing data.
mis.good: We can leverage our existing data.
mis.why: 'Leverage' is a transitive verb here; no 'of'.

def: To make sure that plans or ideas agree with each other.
ex: We need to align our goals with the company strategy.
nat: Let's meet to align on priorities before the launch.

mis.bad: We need to align about the priorities.
mis.good: We need to align on the priorities.
mis.why: Use 'align on' a topic or 'align with' a person or plan.

def: The range of work or topics that a project covers.
ex: The scope of the project grew without extra budget.
nat: Adding new features is outside the scope of this contract.

mis.bad: This is out of the scope.
mis.good: This is out of scope.
mis.why: Say 'out of scope' (no 'the') or 'outside the scope'.

def: Feeling that there is too much to deal with.
ex: I feel overwhelmed by the number of emails I get.
nat: She was overwhelmed with work after the merger.

mis.bad: I am overwhelmed of work.
mis.good: I am overwhelmed with work.

def: Able to be trusted to work well or do what is promised.
ex: We need a reliable internet connection for the call.
nat: He is a reliable colleague who always meets deadlines.

mis.bad: The system is confiable.
mis.good: The system is reliable.

def: Working well without wasting time, money, or effort.
ex: The new process is much more efficient than the old one.
nat: An efficient team can finish the task in half the time.

mis.bad: We need a more efficient way of work.
mis.good: We need a more efficient way to work.
mis.why: Use 'way to + verb' to say how to do something.

def: Leaving very little time, money, or space.
ex: We are working to a tight schedule this month.
nat: The budget is tight, so we can't hire anyone new.

mis.bad: We have a short deadline.
mis.good: We have a tight deadline.
mis.why: 'Short deadline' is understood, but 'tight deadline' is the natural collocation.

def: A belief about how something will or should happen.
ex: The product did not meet our expectations.
nat: It's important to set clear expectations with the client.

mis.bad: I have expectative of a raise.
mis.good: I have expectations of a raise.

def: A problem that delays or stops progress.
ex: The server failure was a major setback for the project.
nat: Despite the setback, we launched on schedule.

mis.bad: We had a set back in the project.
mis.good: We had a setback in the project.
mis.why: As a noun, 'setback' is one word.

def: Still happening or continuing now.
ex: We have an ongoing investigation into the issue.
nat: There are ongoing talks between the two companies.

mis.bad: The project is in going.
mis.good: The project is ongoing.

def: Done carefully and completely, with attention to detail.
ex: The team did a thorough review of the code.
nat: She gave a thorough explanation of the new process.

mis.bad: We did a through analysis.
mis.good: We did a thorough analysis.

def: Not willing to do something and slow to agree.
ex: The client was reluctant to sign without a trial period.
nat: Many managers are reluctant to try new tools.

mis.bad: I am reluctant in doing it.
mis.good: I am reluctant to do it.
